title: Longest Common Prefix After at Most One Removal
statement:
You may delete at most one character of `s` (deleting none is also allowed); the remaining characters keep their order. `t` is never changed.

Return the largest number `L` such that the resulting string and `t` begin with the same `L` characters. `L` is `0` when they cannot even share a first character.
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The brute force deletes each character of `s` in turn (or none) and compares prefixes, which is O(n²). A single pass is enough. While `s` and `t` agree, nothing needs deleting. At the first mismatch, at `s[i]` against `t[j]`, the only repair is a deletion at or before `i`, and deleting `s[i]` itself is never worse than deleting an earlier character: an earlier deletion shifts the part that already matched, while the characters after `i` slide into the same places either way. So two pointers moving in the same direction spend the deletion on the first mismatch, and the second mismatch ends the prefix.

## Approach

1. `i` walks `s`, `j` walks `t`, and `removed` says whether the deletion is used.
2. While both pointers are inside their strings, compare `s[i]` with `t[j]`.
3. If they are equal, advance both pointers.
4. If not and the deletion is unused, delete `s[i]`: set `removed` and advance only `i`.
5. If not and the deletion is already used, stop.
6. Return `j`, the number of characters of `t` matched.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "madxa"`, `t = "madam"`. The letters `m`, `a`, `d` match, so `i = j = 3`. Then `s[3] = 'x'` differs from `t[3] = 'a'`: the deletion is spent on `x` and `i` becomes 4. Now `s[4] = 'a'` matches `t[3]`, giving `i = 5` and `j = 4`. `s` is used up, so the answer is `4` (`"mada"`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), where n is `s.length`: every step moves `i` forward, so the loop runs at most n times.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Only `s` loses a character, never `t`: for `s = "b"`, `t = "ab"` the answer is `0`.
- There is only one deletion; at the second mismatch stop instead of skipping again.
- Return `j`, not `i`: `i` also counts the deleted character.
- When either string runs out, the prefix simply ends there; a deletion cannot lengthen it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | current position in `s` |
| `j` | current position in `t`, which is also the length matched so far |
| `removed` | whether the one allowed deletion has been used |

narration.3: j walks through t and counts how many of its characters are matched.
narration.4: The one allowed deletion has not been used yet.
narration.5: Compare while both strings still have characters left.
narration.9: A mismatch, and the deletion is still free.
narration.10: Spend it on s[i]: deleting the mismatching character keeps the matched part intact.
narration.11: Skip that character of s; t[j] waits for the next character of s.
narration.13: A second mismatch cannot be repaired, so the common prefix ends here.
narration.16: j characters of t were matched: that is the longest common prefix.
